title: What Do People Think About?
gist: A short teaser for a new study by economists at Claremont Graduate University and Wuhan University that maps the recurring subjects of everyday human thought and sorts thinking styles into four buckets; the visible text stops before the four buckets are named, but flags that coffee and cats outrank sex in frequency and that thought content is understudied relative to its effect on self-reported happiness.

insights.claim: Economists at Claremont Graduate University and Wuhan University have published a study that identifies patterns in the subjects people think about most and sorts human thinking styles into four discrete buckets.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: A four-type taxonomy of thought content is the kind of segmentation consumer-attention, wellness-app and ad-targeting businesses monetize; watch for the typology to be productized.
insights.quote: identifies patterns in the subjects people turn to most frequently and sorts human thinking styles into four buckets
insights.locator: Given the general inscrutability of thought

insights.claim: In the study's ranking of what occupies everyday human thought, sex barely registers while coffee and cats rank higher.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Mundane consumables, not primal drives, dominate mental share-of-voice — a useful corrective for anyone modeling consumer attention or advertising salience.
insights.quote: Sex barely made the list. Coffee and cats fared better.
insights.locator: Psychology / What Do People Think About? dek

insights.claim: The contents of human thought are surprisingly understudied despite their documented impact on self-reported happiness, leaving an open research field that economists rather than psychologists are now entering.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Wellbeing measurement is migrating from psychology into economics; expect thought-content metrics to start appearing in happiness and policy indices.
insights.quote: the contents of our thoughts are surprisingly understudied

insights.claim: Even people who know each other well cannot infer the actual content of one another's thoughts, and most individuals have only a weak handle on where their own minds go day to day.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Self-report and inferred-intent data are structurally noisy — a caution for any model that assumes revealed preference maps cleanly onto mental state.
insights.quote: it’s impossible to know what is actually going through their heads
insights.locator: But many people have only a glancing handle
